claims.text: An active-learning ML interatomic potential can be combined with multi-step thermodynamic integration and importance sampling.
The proposed ML-IAP can be trained to capture vibrational dynamics, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The combined workflow will substantially reduce the cost of calculating solid and liquid free-energy landscapes.
The workflow can calculate derived fusion properties such as melting temperature and latent heat.
The workflow will be at least ten times faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Predicted melting temperatures will deviate by less than approximately 5% from full ab initio benchmarks.
Predicted latent heats will deviate by less than approximately 5% from full ab initio benchmarks.
The ML-IAP inherently captures the atomic-scale vibrational dynamics and electron–vibration interactions governing accurate solid–liquid free-energy differences.
ML potentials can reproduce underlying DFT energies and forces with near-DFT accuracy while offering a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
Low-cost ML evaluations can faithfully reproduce the energetic and entropic contributions needed for phase free energies.
Using the ML potential in thermodynamic integration will reduce the amount of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics sampling required.
The workflow will preserve the vibrational and anharmonic fidelity required for precise free-energy calculations.
The workflow will perform better than TOR-TILD for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The method is applicable to elemental metals, binary alloys, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The intended temperature range is approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature.
Validation will proceed from elemental and binary systems to a representative high-entropy alloy.
The hypothesis is falsified if phase free energies or derived observables differ from full ab initio molecular-dynamics benchmarks by more than 5%.
The hypothesis is falsified if computational time is not reduced by at least one order of magnitude.
